tests.title: SMT scaling (fp32 FMA)
tests.description: Whether the CPU's extra hardware threads (SMT, or Intel's Hyper-Threading) add throughput, on two maths kernels each run once with one thread per physical core and again on every thread the chip offers. The first keeps enough independent calculations in flight to fill a core from one thread, so a second thread usually adds nothing; the second is one long chain where each step waits for the last, which leaves a core mostly idle for a second thread to use.

metrics.description: One thread per physical core, with the extra hardware threads left idle. Each thread keeps enough independent calculations in flight to fill its core on its own.

Every hardware thread busy, including the second thread sharing each core. Matching the one-thread-per-core reading is the usual result: that thread had already filled the core, so the second one can only share it.
One thread per physical core running a single chain, where each step waits for the one before it -- so the core's maths units sit idle most of the time.

Every hardware thread running a single chain. The second thread on each core fills the idle time the first leaves, which is the case SMT is built for: expect close to twice the one-thread-per-core chain.

tests.title: DRAM bandwidth
tests.description: How many bytes per second all cores together can move to and from main memory. The arrays are far too big for any cache, so every access goes out to RAM. The two rows that write count only the bytes the program asked for, the usual STREAM convention; most CPUs must also fetch each line before overwriting it, so copy and triad move about half again as much as they count and normally land below the read row.

metrics.description: Reading one large array straight through, start to end.
Copying one large array into another -- a read and a write for every element.
Scaling one array, adding a second and storing to a third: two reads and a write per element, the hardest of the three.

tests.title: Cache bandwidth (read)
tests.description: How many bytes per second the CPU can read out of each cache, from the tiny fast one next to the core to the big slow one shared by all of them. Each reading uses a working set sized to stay inside the cache it names.

metrics.description: One thread reading from the small cache inside its own core.
Every core reading from its own L1 at the same time.
One thread reading from the mid-level cache, the next step out.
Every core reading from L2 at once; where L2 is shared, the data is split between them so it still fits.
One thread reading from the large cache shared by all cores.
Every core reading from that shared cache at once, each taking a slice of it.

tests.title: L1 bandwidth (write / copy)
tests.description: How many bytes per second a core can write into its nearest cache, and copy within it. Cores have fewer paths out to memory than in, so writing usually lands below the matching read row.

metrics.description: One thread storing new values into its own L1.
Every core storing into its own L1 at the same time.
One thread copying inside L1 -- one read plus one write for every byte moved.
Every core copying inside its own L1 at the same time.

tests.title: Memory latency (pointer-chase)
tests.description: How long the core waits for one memory read when it has nothing else to do -- each read's address comes from the previous read, so the hardware cannot start the next one early.

metrics.description: Reading from the small cache inside the core.
Reading from the mid-level cache, after an L1 miss.
Reading from the last-level cache shared between cores.
Reading from main memory at random -- the worst case.
Main memory again, but read in address order, so the hardware can fetch ahead -- the best case DRAM gets.
Eight independent chases at once: the reads overlap instead of waiting in turn, so each costs less.
Thirty-two chases at once -- deep enough that the core runs out of room for further overlap, so the cost per read stops falling.
The address-translation cost on its own: the data is cached, but every read lands on a different page.

tests.title: Atomic fetch-add latency
tests.description: How long one all-or-nothing counter update takes. This is the operation behind locks, reference counts and every shared data structure, so it sets the cost of coordinating between threads.

metrics.description: One thread updating a counter nobody else touches, so it stays in that core's own cache.
